title: Statistical Comparisons of Classifiers over Multiple Data Sets
problem_statement: Comparing the performance of machine learning classifiers across multiple benchmark datasets is a fundamental task in empirical machine learning research, yet researchers frequently apply inappropriate parametric tests such as paired t-tests or uncorrected all-pairs comparisons whose statistical assumptions are severely violated.
domain: Machine Learning Evaluation and Applied Statistics
theoretical_framework: Non-parametric statistical hypothesis testing, ranking-based comparison procedures (Wilcoxon signed-ranks test, Friedman test with Iman-Davenport correction), and family-wise error rate control methodologies (Bonferroni-Dunn, Holm, Hochberg, Hommel) under non-normal score distributions and incommensurable measurement scales.
methodology: The author theoretically reviews parametric and non-parametric statistical procedures and empirically analyzes their behavior across 40 real-world benchmark classification datasets from the UCI repository. The analysis evaluates two-classifier comparison methods (paired t-test on absolute differences, paired t-test on relative differences, Wilcoxon signed-ranks test, and sign test) and multiple-classifier comparison methods (repeated-measures ANOVA with Tukey and Dunnett post-hoc tests, Friedman test with Nemenyi, Bonferroni-Dunn, Holm step-down, Hochberg step-up, and Hommel post-hoc procedures). The empirical framework simulates researcher selection bias using a logistic sampling function across 1,000 resamples of 10 datasets, evaluates statistical power (rejection frequencies and mean p-values) and replicability (outcome-based R(e) and variance-based R(p)), and introduces Critical Difference (CD) diagrams for visual ranking representation.
datasets: 40 UCI Machine Learning Repository benchmark datasets (adult, balance-scale, bands, breast cancer (haberman), breast cancer (lju), breast cancer (wisc), car evaluation, contraceptive method choice, credit screening, dermatology, ecoli, glass identification, hayesroth, hepatitis, housing, imports-85, ionosphere, iris, liver disorders, lung cancer, lymphography, mushrooms, pima indians diabetes, post-operative, primary tumor, promoters, rheumatism, servo, shuttle landing, soybean, spambase, spect, spectf, teaching assistant evaluation, tic tac toe, titanic, voting, waveform, wine recognition, yeast)

metrics: Area Under the ROC Curve (AUC, 5-fold cross-validation)
evaluated_statistical_tests: Sign test (counts of wins, ties, losses)
Repeated-measures ANOVA (with Tukey and Dunnett post-hoc tests)
evaluated_learning_algorithms: C4.5 decision tree (with default and tuned m / cf hyperparameters)
Naive Bayes with LOESS continuous probability modeling
k-Nearest Neighbors (k=10 with Gaussian kernel weighting)

key_findings: Non-parametric tests (Wilcoxon signed-ranks test for two classifiers and Friedman test with post-hoc tests for multiple classifiers) should be preferred over parametric tests (paired t-test and repeated-measures ANOVA) for comparing classifiers over multiple datasets.
Parametric tests rely on assumptions of normal distribution and sphericity/homogeneity of variance, which are routinely violated by classifier performance metrics across diverse benchmark datasets.

The Wilcoxon signed-ranks test achieves higher statistical power (lower average p-values and higher null-hypothesis rejection rates) and superior variance-based replicability R(p) compared to paired t-tests across 40 UCI benchmark datasets.
The Iman-Davenport F_F statistic resolves the severe conservatism of the standard Friedman chi-squared statistic.

When comparing multiple algorithms against a single control classifier, post-hoc procedures such as Bonferroni-Dunn, Holm, and Hochberg provide substantially greater statistical power than all-to-all Nemenyi comparisons by evaluating only k-1 hypotheses instead of k(k-1)/2 hypotheses.
Critical Difference (CD) diagrams effectively summarize average classifier ranks and statistically significant pairwise differences in a compact graphical format.
Filtering comparisons to count only statistically significant wins and losses degrades test reliability by establishing an arbitrary p < 0.05 threshold.
scope_and_delimitations: Delimited to evaluating classifier comparison methods across multiple independent datasets rather than assessing within-dataset variance or cross-validation fold dependencies.
Treated dataset scores as reliable point estimates without modeling the covariance or variance of individual training-test splits.
Restricted empirical simulations to 40 classification benchmark datasets from the UCI repository with discrete class attributes.
Simulated algorithm performance differences by varying dataset selection probabilities via a logistic bias function k over 1,000 resamples of 10 datasets.

limitations.verbatim_excerpt: In the empirical study we provided no analysis of Type 1/Type 2 error rates. The main reason for this is that the correct result—rejection or non-rejection of the null-hypothesis—is not well defined and depends upon the kind of difference between the algorithms we intend to measure. Besides, conducting the experiments in which we knew the true hypotheses would require artificial data sets and classifiers with the prescribed probabilities and distributions of errors. For this we would need to make some assumptions about the real-world distributions; these assumptions are, however, exactly what we were testing in the first place.
limitations.summary: The author acknowledges that the empirical simulation did not measure Type I and Type II error rates because defining ground-truth hypotheses would require synthetic datasets with predetermined distributions, which would undermine evaluating whether real-world data conforms to test assumptions. Additionally, the non-parametric framework cannot incorporate cross-validation fold variance due to overlapping training samples, and post-hoc tests may occasionally fail to pinpoint significant pairs despite omnibus Friedman significance.

generalizability_gap: The empirical simulations evaluated only 40 discrete-target classification datasets from the UCI repository and classical learners (decision trees, Naive Bayes, kNN); the study did not empirically test regression algorithms, unsupervised models, structured output predictors, or modern deep learning architectures across large-scale heterogeneous benchmarks.
methodological_gap: The proposed non-parametric framework cannot model within-dataset sample variance or repeated cross-validation fold covariance because training data overlaps across folds, and omnibus Friedman significance does not guarantee that post-hoc tests will have sufficient statistical power to identify specific differing pairs.
